subject: Computer Networking
title: Microservices and the Web
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Microservices and the Web.

hook.text: One giant app does everything. It breaks, and everything goes down. Microservices split the work up.

buildup.text: Each microservice handles one task: auth, payments, search. They communicate via APIs over HTTP or gRPC.

discovery.text: Teams deploy services independently. Update search without touching payments. Faster releases.

twist.text: Microservices add complexity: service discovery, distributed tracing, and network failures between services.

climax.text: Netflix runs 700+ microservices. Amazon has thousands. Scale demands decomposition.

punchline.text: Microservices trade monolith simplicity for scale and speed.

quiz.question: What is a key advantage of microservices over a monolith?
options: Services can be deployed and updated independently
They eliminate the need for APIs

details.summary: Microservices architecture decomposes web applications into small, independent services that communicate over HTTP and messaging. Each service owns its data and can be deployed, scaled, and updated independently. This enables large teams to work in parallel without coordination bottlenecks.
details.whyItMatters: Microservices enable the scale and velocity that large web applications require. Understanding their trade-offs explains why companies like Netflix and Amazon adopted this architecture.
takeaways: Each service is independently deployable and scalable
Services communicate over HTTP/REST, gRPC, or message queues
Independent deployment enables frequent releases without coordination

faq.question: When are microservices the right choice?
faq.answer: Microservices suit large applications with multiple teams where independent deployment and scaling are needed. For small teams and simple applications, a monolith is faster to develop and operate. Most projects should start as monoliths and extract services only when complexity demands it.

faq.question: What are the downsides of microservices?
faq.answer: Distributed systems are fundamentally harder to debug, monitor, and test. Network calls between services add latency. Data consistency across service boundaries requires careful design. Operational complexity increases with more services. These overhead costs only pay off at significant scale.
